current.answer:
Standard disclosure is the disclosure order under CPR Part 31 where a party must disclose only the documents on which it relies, the documents that adversely affect its own case or another party’s case, the documents that support another party’s case, and any documents required by a relevant practice direction. [4]

To give standard disclosure, the party must make a reasonable search for those documents, and the reasonableness of the search depends on factors such as the number of documents, the nature and complexity of the case, the ease and expense of retrieval, and the significance of any likely documents. [5]

After the search, the party must make a list of the documents it knows about that fall within rule 31.6 and that are or have been in its control, unless rule 31.10(8) applies. [9]

The list should be in Form N265. [11]

The retrieved material is **court-specific**, and it does not by itself establish the general CPR position. [1]

For appeals to the Court of Appeal Civil Division, you generally must file an appellant’s notice within the time directed by the lower court or, if none is given, within 21 days of the date of the decision being appealed. [1]

In the Court of Appeal, the shortest time limit mentioned in the guide is 7 days from the date of the decision in some specific cases. [2]

In the Commercial Court, the guide says challenges to an award are subject to a 28-day period fixed by section 70(3) of the 1996 Act, but the court can vary that period and will require cogent reasons for extending time. [3]

In the Senior Courts Costs Office, the guide says an appeal notice must generally be filed within 21 days after the date of the decision appealed against. [5]

The Senior Courts Costs Office guide also says that if a detailed assessment is carried out at more than one hearing, time for appeal does not start until the conclusion of the final hearing unless the court orders otherwise. [5]

If you want the general CPR time limit, please ask for the specific procedure, such as “appealing,” “appeal to the Court of Appeal,” or “costs appeal,” because the current sources are from different court guides. [1]

Under CPR 2.8, periods expressed in days are calculated as clear days, the first day is not counted, and if the period is 5 days or less, Saturdays, Sundays, Bank Holidays, Christmas Day and Good Friday do not count. [5]

CPR 2.8 also says that if time for an act at court office ends on a day when the office is closed, the act is in time if done on the next day the office is open. [5]

Under CPR 2.9, where the court sets a time limit, the last date for compliance should, where practicable, be expressed as a calendar date and include the time of day. [6]

The Commercial Court Guide says the court can vary the 28-day period fixed by section 70(3) of the 1996 Act, but any challenge to an award should be pursued without delay and the court will require cogent reasons for extending time. [1]
